<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-module.md -->

# First Module

Modules change particle values over time. A custom module receives the live
particle, the frame delta, and a shared execution context.

```ts
import { Module } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const riseAndFade = new Module((particle, deltaTime) => {
  particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  particle.alpha *= 1 - particle.time;
});
```

Attach it to a system with the rest of your modules:

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules: [riseAndFade],
  renderers,
});
```

Use `condition` when only some particles should be affected:

```ts
const sparksOnly = new Module((particle) => {
  particle.scale.multiplyScalar(1.2);
}, {
  condition: (particle) => particle.tags?.includes("spark") ?? false,
});
```

The exported `ModuleCondition` type receives the same arguments as `ModuleUpdate`:
`(particle, deltaTime, context)`, and returns a boolean. The context exposes the owning `system`,
`deltaTime`, a read-only `events` batch, and the optional managed `octree`. Preparation, conditions,
and particle callbacks share one context for the execution. Conditions run after alive and tag
filtering. Callbacks can omit arguments they do not need. On GPU, `ModuleGPUCondition` matches
`ModuleGPUUpdate`'s arguments and returns a TSL boolean node; its context exposes the managed
`spatialGrid` and native event batch.

This major release replaces the former `(particle, deltaTime, system?, octree?)` signature.
Move system and spatial queries into the context; class preparation now receives `prepare(context)`.
There is one callback path for both function-defined and class-based modules.

Declare `events` and optionally `eventScope` in module options to receive subscribed events. Modules default to
`'local'`; use `'parent'` for the immediate parent only, or an array such as `['local', 'parent']` to combine origins.
The batch is frozen before preparation and stays the same through conditions and particle updates.
Events emitted during those callbacks remain pending until a subsequent execution. Use the preparation
hook to interpret a batch once when the result can be shared across particles.

For performance-sensitive modules, avoid allocating objects inside the per
particle callback. Reuse vectors and colors outside the callback when possible.

A plain Module defaults to permanent priority. The example's velocity increment accumulates over time; multiplying by
delta seconds makes 0.5 an acceleration rather than an amount per frame. Its alpha multiplication also accumulates. For
a fade defined entirely by normalized age, prefer ColorOverLifetime or set `priority: Module.Priority.Transient` so the
fade is reapplied to cached base alpha each frame.

Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` when a temporary velocity adjustment must affect this frame's integration.
Render-time transient modules run after movement. See [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) before combining several
modules that assign the same property.

## Particle Initialization

Use `initializeParticle(particle, context)` to establish state once after emitter attributes are
assigned, before the first simulation/render and before external spawn listeners. Hooks follow
configured module order and tag filters, independently of update priority and update conditions.
They run for ordinary and subsystem births. Initialization is distinct from subscribed events.
Both hooks default to `undefined`; modules without an initializer do no birth-hook work.
CPU-only initializers require CPU processing unless `initializeParticleGPU` is also provided.

```ts
const birthMass = new Module(() => {}, {
  initializeParticle(particle, context) {
    particle.mass = context.event ? 2 : 1;
  },
  initializeParticleGPU(particle, context) {
    particle.mass.assign(context.event ? 2 : 1);
  },
  modifyGPU() {},
});
```

The CPU context exposes `system`, optional `source` and the original triggering `event`.
The GPU context provides node-compatible source attributes and event snapshots; native hooks
execute inline in the emission kernel without readback. A CPU-only initializer requires a GPU
implementation before native GPU simulation is supported. Class-based modules can override the
same methods. GPU hook JavaScript constructs a compute graph, so use TSL operations for
per-particle branches and mutations.

`sourceToWorld` interprets source/event simulation coordinates. `birthToWorld` interprets the
newborn attributes at initialization, including Source-space births that will subsequently be
resolved through their source frame. Hooks that calculate world-space coordinates should use
these supplied frames. See [material copying](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/material-copying.html) for a built-in initializer.

## System Update Hooks

`prepare(context)` can also run effect-level scheduling once per simulation step, even when a module does
not modify individual particles. Supply an empty CPU callback and `modifyGPU() {}` to keep both backends supported,
then put the shared scheduling work in `prepare(context)`. Read `context.system` and `context.deltaTime` there. Call
`super.prepare(context)` to preserve the base preparation behavior.
Function-defined modules can supply the same hook as an option:

```ts
const scheduler = new Module(() => {}, {
  prepare({ system, deltaTime }) {
    // Advance application scheduling on the simulation clock.
    advanceSchedule(system, deltaTime);
  },
  modifyGPU() {},
});
```

This follows the system's pause state, simulation speed and fixed-step advancement.

[Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html) uses this pattern to schedule independent bubble events from persistent decal sources.
Its per-particle callbacks intentionally do nothing. The demo factory returns a ParticleSystem, so this hook lets it
keep scheduling on the system's clock without owning an animation loop. Applications with their own animation loop
can instead schedule events there before calling the root system's update().

## Managed Octree

Particle-to-particle comparisons should use a managed `ParticleOctree` instead of scanning the
whole particle array for every particle. Enable it in the module options; RZMPS rebuilds it and
exposes it through `context.octree` in preparation, conditions, and particle callbacks.

```ts
const crowdDrag = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, { octree }) => {
    const nearbyCount = octree
      .particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2)
      .filter((neighbor) => neighbor !== particle)
      .length;
    const damping = Math.max(0, 1 - nearbyCount * 0.02 * deltaTime);
    particle.velocity.multiplyScalar(damping);
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    octreeOptions: {
      maxDepth: 6,
      particlesPerLeaf: 8,
    },
  },
);
```

The octree owns its default aggregator, which returns an empty object for every node.
Supply `octreeAggregator` when a module needs custom aggregate data, such as a count or average velocity.

The octree prunes nodes outside the query sphere, then returns the particles that pass exact
distance checks in the remaining leaves. Custom aggregate data remains useful when an
approximation such as average position or velocity is cheaper than collecting every matching
particle; see
[particle spatial acceleration](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/particle-octree.html).

For reusable behavior, extend Module and pass your per-particle callback and options to `super`. Override
`prepare(context)` when expensive shared work should happen once per frame; call `super.prepare` if using
automatic spatial-effect collection. Put resource cleanup in `cleanup()`. Dependencies in `dependents` participate in
normal priority sorting rather than forcing an independent update loop.

Built-in modules already cover forces, noise, scale, rotation, depth, color, and collision. Reuse those when their
semantics match the effect. Custom callbacks are most useful for application-specific logic, and should mutate the
particle provided rather than storing a shared mutable vector in multiple particles.

The callback above is CPU-only. Continue with [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) to add the
equivalent TSL operation, then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for managed
spatial queries, invalidation, and testing requirements.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-spatial-effect.md -->

# First Spatial Effect

Spatial effects modify particles based on scene-space volumes or custom tests.
Use a built-in force field when particles should react to an area in the scene.

```ts
import * as THREE from "three";
import { ParticleForceField } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const updraft = ParticleForceField.Sphere({
  direction: new THREE.Vector3(0, 2, 0),
}, 2);

updraft.position.set(0, 1, 0);
scene.add(updraft);
```

Particle systems discover generic spatial effects in their scene by default.
Disable that behavior per system with `useSpatialEffects: false`, or use
`spatialEffectFilter` to choose which effects apply.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  spatialEffectFilter: (effect) => effect.name === "updraft",
});
```

Use `KillZone` when particles should be removed inside a volume:

```ts
import { KillZone } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const cleanup = KillZone.Box(10, 4, 10);
cleanup.position.y = -3;
scene.add(cleanup);
```

Name the updraft (`updraft.name = 'updraft'`) before using the filter shown above. A filter cannot find an unnamed field by that name. The direction vector supplies acceleration while the field applies its timestep. In custom callbacks, multiply acceleration by deltaTime before adding it to velocity.

For a custom volume modifier, use `SpatialEffect.Box((particle, deltaTime) => { ... }, options, width, height, depth)`. Scale and position it like another Object3D. A custom `test` option can replace the geometric inclusion rule, while `inverted` applies to the opposite side of a volume. Choose a permanent priority for forces and a transient priority for temporary color or scale changes.

Scene discovery and module-level collections serve different purposes. A generic field modifies intersecting particles directly; a specialized affector can instead be collected by a module such as Boids. See [spatial collections](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/spatial-effects.html) for explicit selection and filtering, and [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) for execution phases.

Custom CPU callbacks do not translate into shader code. Continue with
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) to pair this volume with a TSL modifier,
then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for batching and moving-geometry
policies.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/gpu-processing.md -->

# GPU Processing and Extension Development

RZMPS keeps the same `ParticleSystem` composition on CPU and GPU: emitters create particles,
modules and spatial effects modify them, and renderers display them. Set `gpuProcessing: true`
(the default) and render the system once with an initialized Three.js `WebGPURenderer` to make
GPU simulation eligible. `isGPUProcessingActive` reports the backend actually selected for the
current system; `gpuProcessing` only expresses the requested mode.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters: [emitter],
  modules: [force, color],
  renderers: [sprites],
  gpuProcessing: true,
});

scene.add(particles);
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  particles.update();
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});
```

WebGL always uses CPU simulation. A WebGPU system also uses CPU simulation when GPU processing is
disabled, a module lacks a GPU implementation, GPU tag capacity is exceeded, or a CPU-input
renderer is combined with a render-time modifier. Unsupported generic spatial effects are skipped
by the GPU path rather than moving the entire system to CPU. Inspect `supportsGPU`,
`getGPUEmissionSupport()`, `getGPUExecutionSchedule()`, and `isGPUProcessingActive` when composing
custom components. Changing `gpuProcessing` starts a fresh run because CPU objects and GPU buffers
are separate authoritative states.

## Writing CPU and GPU Modules

The CPU callback mutates a JavaScript `Particle`. `modifyGPU` builds a Three.js Shading Language
(TSL) graph over a `GPUParticleLike`; it does not execute once per particle in JavaScript. Work
through [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) for a complete paired implementation and
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) for influence, feathering, and custom test
rules.

Reuse ordinary CPU hooks for setup and cleanup. `prepare(context)` runs once before a
module's work on either backend. A function-defined module can request managed acceleration with
`useOctree`/`octreeOptions` for CPU or `useSpatialGrid`/`spatialGridOptions` for GPU; the resulting
`ParticleOctree` is available as `context.octree` on CPU; the GPU context exposes `context.spatialGrid`.
Both callbacks use `(particle, deltaTime, context)`, as do their conditions.
`cleanup()` must call `super.cleanup()` when overridden so managed references are released.

`ParticleSpatialGrid` hashes occupied fine cells; it does not allocate a dense world-volume grid.
Its cached build kernels dispatch over `buffers.count`, not reserved capacity, and are submitted
together. A compact GPU-produced population can pass a `GPUComputeRange` as the fourth argument to
`rebuild(renderer, buffers, buildToken, range)`. The range pairs a uint count node with caller-owned
indirect compute arguments (`ceil(count / 64), 1, 1`), written by an earlier GPU scheduling pass.
No count readback is required. `grid.computeParticles(callback, range)` reuses that dispatch
contract for additional kernels, including exact partial-workgroup guarding. Without a range,
the returned kernel uses the current CPU count; update its `count` when that population changes.
Callbacks decide whether dead slots participate. These kernels require an initialized grid and
must be rebuilt if the grid's underlying particle storage is replaced.

### Spatial Aggregation And Levels

`SpatialAggregator<T, "cpu">` preserves the octree's existing `new` and `combine` members
and optionally adds `finalize`. Parent reductions retain raw values. `getAggregate(node)`
finalizes a copy, so deriving averages does not overwrite sums used by other nodes.
CPU values remain ordinary objects; they do not require GPU layouts. Keep finalized state
copyable; native data containers, ordinary object graphs and classes with `clone()` are supported.

`SpatialAggregator<Layout, "gpu">` uses the same concepts with explicit channel types and
TSL expressions. Layout channels support `float`, `uint`, `int`, `vec2`, `vec3` and `vec4`.
Combine raw sums/counts associatively; derive means or normalized vectors in `finalize`.
GPU finalization operates on local expressions, leaving stored raw reductions intact.

```ts
const grid = new ParticleSpatialGrid({ levels: SpatialLevels.All }, {
  layout: { count: 'uint', sum: 'vec3' },
  new: particle => ({
    count: uint(particle ? 1 : 0),
    sum: particle?.position ?? vec3(0),
  }),
  combine: (a, b) => ({ count: a.count.add(b.count), sum: a.sum.add(b.sum) }),
  finalize: a => ({ count: a.count, sum: a.sum.div(float(a.count).max(1)) }),
});
grid.rebuild(renderer, buffers);
const readRegions = grid.computeRegions(0, region => {
  const average = grid.getAggregate(region);
  const bounds = grid.getBounds(region);
  const children = grid.getChildren(region);
  // Consume these GPU expressions in your compute graph; they are not synchronous CPU values.
});
```

Import the TSL constructors from `three/tsl`, and `ParticleSpatialGrid`/`SpatialLevels`
from RZMPS. GPU aggregate callbacks construct graphs, not JavaScript particle callbacks.
The fixed layout and callbacks are construction-time configuration; use captured uniforms
for runtime numeric tuning. Callers own and dispose compute kernels returned by the grid.

Let B be `brickSubdivisions` and D be B plus `cellSubdivisions`:

| `levels` | Maintained depths |
| --- | --- |
| `SpatialLevels.None` / `"none"` / `"None"`, default | D only |
| `SpatialLevels.Bricks` / `"bricks"` / `"Bricks"` | 0 through B, plus D |
| `SpatialLevels.Cells` / `"cells"` / `"Cells"` | B through D |
| `SpatialLevels.All` / `"*"` / `"All"` | 0 through D |
| Readonly integer array | Requested depths plus D, sorted and deduplicated |

Both brick/cell presets include B. Invalid depths or presets throw rather than silently
clamping. The finest neighbor-query index is always present. Ordinary default/None grids
without an aggregator allocate no extra region directories. A non-None preset, explicit
depth array, or aggregator enables the optional sparse region directory; aggregate storage
is allocated only when an aggregator is supplied. Managed grids share only compatible levels.

Region handles are frame-local GPU expressions with a `valid` flag. `locateNode(position, depth)`
finds an occupied region at a maintained depth; outside or empty regions are invalid.
`getRegions(depth)` gives a GPU count and ordinal-to-region accessor; `computeRegions`
dispatches only occupied regions. Requesting an unmaintained depth throws, rather than reporting
an empty level. `getChildren` means the **next maintained finer level**, not necessarily depth+1.
Repeat child traversal to reach occupied descendants without scanning every region at that depth.
At the finest level, `getParticleIndices` gives the region's particle membership range.

CPU octree handles are ordinary node references. Its existing `locate` returns the deepest
available containing node up to the requested depth, with the existing root fallback outside
bounds; grid `locate(Vector3, depth)` remains a CPU coordinate utility, not a GPU lookup.
Both structures provide `getAggregate`, `getBounds` and `getChildren` where those concepts agree.
Neither node references nor GPU region indices should be retained across rebuilds.

Additional grid levels use exact sparse cell keys, compact occupied-cell lists and child
ranges. The finest summaries are constructed once; coarser levels combine raw child summaries.
No dense world-volume arrays or separate pointer-based GPU octree are constructed. Hash-table
capacity clearing remains allocation-sized, while scans and aggregate work use occupied counts.

Dynamic numbers, vectors, colors, ranges, sets, and callbacks are available to built-in GPU
components. Callback curves are sampled into interpolated uniform tables at
`ParticleSystem.Settings.GPU_DYNAMIC_VALUE_RESOLUTION`; increase it when a high-frequency curve needs more
fidelity. TSL nodes can be supplied directly where a dynamic value is evaluated by GPU code.

## Emitters and Spatial Effects

Built-in GPU emission supports rate, distance rate, timed bursts, tags, initial values, LOD, and
volume, surface, or vertex sampling from buffer geometry. CPU and GPU volume emission share the
shape's baked Halton sample table. `volumeSamples` is `"auto"` by default; assigning a number fixes
the table size, while changing geometry or the sample setting rebuilds it. Surface selection is
weighted by triangle area. Burst times are normalized emission-cycle values from 0 through 1.

Emitters use the built-in GPU birth pipeline; they are configured through `Emitter` and
`EmissionShape`, not extended with a separate shader callback. Custom behavior belongs in a
module or spatial effect after birth.

Custom `SpatialEffect` implementations pair the CPU `modify`, `condition`, and `test` callbacks
with `modifyGPU`, `conditionGPU`, and `testGPU`. The GPU test returns a float influence from 0 to 1,
which supplies feather strength to `modifyGPU`. Built-in analytic volumes are batched and indexed.
Custom geometry uses a baked field, controlled by `bakedFieldResolution`; set `updatePolicy` to
`Static`, `TransformDynamic`, or `GeometryDynamic` when automatic change detection is not the best
fit. Custom tests are not bounds-filtered because RZMPS cannot assume they depend on geometry.

## Renderers, Events, and Readback

GPU-native renderers override `_updateGPU` and consume `GPUParticleBufferState` or the compact
render-output buffer. A renderer whose implementation needs ordinary `Particle` objects can
override `_updateGPU` and call the protected `updateCPUFromGPU` helper. It selectively reads the
requested fields, ignores overlapping requests while one is pending, and passes the resulting
particles through the renderer's public `update` method. Override `updateGPUUsesCPUReadback` to
keep child expansion on that CPU path:

```ts
class DebugRenderer extends Renderer {
  get updateGPUUsesCPUReadback() { return true; }

  _updateGPU(buffers, system, deltaTime) {
    this.updateCPUFromGPU(
      buffers,
      system,
      deltaTime,
      64,
      ["position", "color", "alpha"],
    );
  }

  _update(particles) {
    // Render the selectively reconstructed Particle objects.
  }
}
```

Request only the slots and fields the renderer actually consumes. Outside a renderer, use the
public system API directly:

```ts
const samples = await system.selectiveReadback(64, ["position", "color", "alpha"]);
```

Readback is delayed and may return no result if its bounded pool is busy. Do not use it to drive
same-frame simulation decisions. Lifecycle and collision events are also delivered asynchronously
from GPU buffers, so listeners and CPU audio/render views can lag simulation slightly. GPU-native
subsystems consume spawn, death, collision, and continuous emission on the GPU; update only the
root system, as on CPU.

Native subsystem births stay within WebGPU's default limit of eight compute-stage storage-buffer
bindings. Parent and child particle state each use separate float and integer buffers. The
remaining pass-specific bindings come from packed allocation state, the emitter-runtime fields
actually referenced by that pass, and packed shape-sampling data. Emitters dispatch separately so
adding emitters does not accumulate their geometry bindings in one shader. Applications do not
need to request a higher device limit.

## Collision and Neighbor Queries

`Collision` selects `ThreeCollisionBackend` for CPU processing and `ThreeGPUCollisionBackend` for
GPU processing when no backend is supplied. An explicit CPU-only backend makes the module GPU
incompatible. GPU collision does not support applying impulses back to scene bodies. Classify GPU
geometry with `CollisionGeometryUpdatePolicy`: static geometry is built once, transform-dynamic
geometry updates transforms, and geometry-dynamic meshes refit or rebuild changed acceleration
data.

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU neighbor work and `ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU queries. A grid query
emits TSL and invokes its visitor in shader code; it does not return JavaScript particles. Bounds
can expand automatically, but a larger volume lowers spatial resolution because the logical cell
count stays fixed. `maxQuerySteps: 0` performs unbounded exact traversal; a positive value is an
explicit performance cap.

## Configuration and Validation

Built-in components synchronize ordinary runtime property changes before each GPU frame. Constant
and sampled value changes update uniforms; structural changes invalidate and rebuild the affected
compute graph or resources. Custom components should expose changed scalar/vector data through
their GPU parameter nodes and set `needsUpdate = true` when changing graph structure, geometry
layout, callback identity, or buffer ownership.

Test both execution paths. WebGPU rendering alone does not prove GPU simulation is active: assert
`isGPUProcessingActive` after rendering has captured its context. Compare CPU and GPU behavior at
fixed timesteps, exercise resets and subsystem events, and inspect `gpuBufferStats`,
`gpuEventStats`, `gpuSpatialStats`, `gpuSelectiveReadbackStats`, and `gpuConfigurationStats` when
profiling. GPU output is expected to be behaviorally equivalent, not bit-for-bit identical.

See [renderer children and population LOD](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/renderer-children-lod.html) for system quality, destructive culling, visual expansion, hierarchy access, and default GPU buffer limits.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/material-copying.md -->

# Material Copying and Compositing

Material copying binds accessible surface inputs to a particle. Compositing combines those inputs
with the renderer's configured material. It copies color, opacity, tangent-space normal maps,
roughness, metalness, and compatible environment inputs; it does not evaluate the source's lighting, custom GLSL, or TSL graph.
Source materials and textures remain caller-owned and unchanged. CPU particle copying vectors allocate only
on first access; ordinary particles, clones, and uploads avoid those allocations. Registered source materials
enable renderer copying without scanning the particle population.

## Environment Maps

Environment textures remain borrowed rather than being baked into the surface atlas. Persistent decals
copy their selected material's `envMap`, `envMapIntensity`, and `envMapRotation` when supported by the
destination material. A live capture keeps updating through that shared texture reference; destroying a
particle system or decal never disposes the source environment texture.

A shared mesh draw uses an explicit `materialTarget` environment, or a compatible environment shared
by the registered copied materials. Distinct captures, intensities, or rotations cannot vary inside one
shared material; that case retains the renderer's configured environment. Decals have independent
materials and can use different captures. Separate renderer tag groups with explicit material targets can select different shared captures.
A particle system's own live cubemap takes precedence on its
mesh renderer. Lit sprites inherit compatible environment maps and intensity unless their own environment
options or system capture override them.

WebGL shaders omit empty atlas channels, reuse destination texture samplers, and use uniforms for a
single-material palette. This leaves texture units available for environment maps, shadow maps, and
light-probe textures; the changes add no GPU storage buffers.
Atlas growth reserves power-of-two tile capacity with spare cells, avoiding rebakes when the next source fits.
Empty atlas channels defer GPU allocation until used unless a minimum capacity is explicitly requested.
Set `atlasOptions: { minCapacity: 4 }` in renderer options to reserve at least four tiles per copied-map channel.
This is a creation-time setting; capacity rounds up to a power of two and can grow beyond that minimum.
In automatic-resolution mode, pixel storage grows when larger source textures arrive.
The underlying `TextureAtlas` option is `minCapacity`, for example `new TextureAtlas({ minCapacity: 4 })`;
its first `update(renderer)` allocates that storage even with no sources, without submitting bake draws.
The same renderer `atlasOptions` configures sprite texture lists and mesh source palettes, including `tileSize` and
`padding`. Copied material channels retain their required color spaces automatically.

By default tiles preserve the largest source texture dimension, up to `atlasOptions.maxTileSize: 2048`.
All tiles in a channel share that resolution; adding a larger image grows the tiles and rebakes existing sources.
An explicit `atlasOptions.tileSize` selects a fixed resolution instead. The complete padded atlas also respects
hardware texture-size limits, reducing tile resolution if necessary. Tiles do not otherwise shrink during use.

Set renderer `textureCopyQuality` to a factor in `(0, 1]` (default `1`) to reduce copied-map resolution before
applying the cap. For example, `textureCopyQuality: 0.5` requests 512-pixel tiles for 1024-pixel source maps.
This creation-time option applies to every copied map channel, including normal and roughness maps, without
modifying the original textures. It also scales an explicit copied-map `tileSize`; sprite texture lists and mesh
source palettes retain their own atlas settings. Use `atlasOptions: { maxTileSize: 512 }` to cap those atlases too.
Borders are extruded and mipmaps are disabled. `TextureAtlas.sample()` retains valid TSL coordinates across
resolution and capacity changes; direct consumers of `rect()` should refresh their rectangles when `version` changes.

Lit WebGL sprites also eliminate absent optional map branches at shader creation, rather than reserving samplers
behind runtime false flags.

`LiveCubemap` remains independent of particle systems: attach it to an object and call `update(scene, renderer, dt)`.
On WebGL it finishes PMREM filtering inside that update and publishes the filtered environment through `map`.
Consumers can keep the same texture reference as captures change, without triggering nested filtering during
material draws. WebGPU keeps its native cube-texture path. `excludeParent` skips the owner during capture;
`dispose()` releases capture/filtering resources and removes the owned cube camera.

## Bind a Surface at Birth

```ts
import { MaterialCopy, MaterialCopySource, MaterialCopySampleMode } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const fragments = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters: new Emitter({ rate: 0, bursts: [{ time: 0, count: 8 }] }),
  modules: [new MaterialCopy({
    source: MaterialCopySource.Collision,
    sampleMode: MaterialCopySampleMode.UVPatch,
  })],
  renderers: new MeshRenderer({ mesh: fragmentMesh }),
});
parent.addSubSystem(fragments, { emitOnCollision: true });
```

The module receives the triggering collision synchronously during initialization, before spawn
listeners, simulation and rendering. It registers the hit material and stores `materialCopy`,
`materialCopyU` and `materialCopyV`. Native GPU births perform the same work in their emission
kernel, retaining event snapshots in the existing run storage without CPU readback or another binding.
The former subsystem `copyCollisionMaterial` option is replaced by this module.

`UVPatch` retains the impact UV and triangle's world-space UV gradients across the fragment's
birth pose. It preserves local texture density, orientation and shear, then travels with the piece.
It approximates one triangle's chart; it cannot reconstruct adjacent triangles, seams or curved surfaces.
Billboards retain density and shear in their sprite plane. `Color` samples each supported map at
the impact UV, while `Texture` uses the particle geometry's own UVs. Color samples stay fixed at
the contact UV even when particles are born away from the contact point. Missing charts fall back to
ordinary texture mapping, or the center sample in Color mode.

Use `source: MaterialCopySource.Event` for event payloads shaped as `MaterialCopyInput`, or
`source: MaterialCopySource.Source` for registered-source `metadata` with that shape. A parent
particle's existing binding can also be inherited through Source mode. A static material or mesh
can be supplied directly as `source`. CPU `resolveSource(particle, context)` and TSL
`resolveSourceGPU(particle, context)` adapt application-specific inputs. Supply both resolvers
when supporting both processing backends. Native custom-event payloads are packed vectors;
use the GPU resolver to interpret `context.event.data` and return a registered binding and chart.

A `MaterialCopyInput` contains `material` (or an existing `materialSourceId`), an optional
`surface: { uv, u, v }`, and `point`. Surface gradients are world-space covectors; `point` is in
`context.sourceToWorld`'s simulation frame. A GPU resolver returns `binding` (ID, U, V, mode),
optional world-space gradients `u`/`v`, and an optional world-space `point`.

Subscribe with the module's existing `events` option to update bindings on later events targeting
the particle. Initialization needs no event subscription and does not wait for event delivery.
See [emission sources and events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) for event timing and payloads.

For a renderer-wide source, use `materialTarget` or `renderer.copyMaterial(material)`;
no MaterialCopy module is required. Sprites, meshes and decals share the appearance pipeline.
Composited decals can also bind their hit surface automatically when neither a particle binding
nor an explicit materialTarget is supplied. Audio and light renderers ignore material compositing.

## Combine Material Inputs

The default combines copied color, opacity, roughness and metalness multiplicatively with the
configured particle material, and perturbs its normal. White and one preserve source values.
A callback overrides only the returned channels; all other channels retain the destination value.
An absent or invalid copied source falls back to the destination inputs.

```ts
const view = new MeshRenderer({
  materialComposite: (source, dest, context) => {
    context.function('blendColor', `
      vec3 blendColor(vec3 source, vec3 dest) { return mix(source, dest, 0.25); }
    `);
    return { color: `blendColor(${source.color}, ${dest.color})`, opacity: dest.opacity };
  },
  materialCompositeGPU: (source, dest) => ({
    color: mix(source.color, dest.color, 0.25),
    opacity: dest.opacity,
  }),
});
```

Import `mix` from `three/tsl` for the GPU example. `materialComposite` builds GLSL expressions;
`materialCompositeGPU` builds TSL nodes. They execute when constructing shaders, not per pixel
in JavaScript. Selection follows the rendering backend: CPU simulation rendered with WebGPU
still uses the TSL callback. Supply both callbacks for applications supporting both renderers.
Assign a new callback to rebuild shaders. If a callback closes over changed configuration, set
`renderer.needsUpdate = true`. GLSL helper names are deduplicated, and conflicting definitions throw.

Color channels use linear RGB. Opacity, roughness and metalness are scalar inputs. Public normal
channels are normalized **view-space** directions: sampled source tangent normals are converted
using the sampled UV chart and destination surface derivatives before compositing. Normalize any
custom normal blend. Source shaders, procedural node outputs and unsupported texture dimensions
are not evaluated. Supported maps use UV0; unavailable maps use neutral samples with the source's
numeric material fields. Normal-map support assumes tangent-space maps.

`context.geometricNormal` supplies the unperturbed view-space normal. Comparing it with the
destination normal can mask a normal-only decal to the pixels that change shading. The lazy
`context.destMapAlpha` multiplies available destination normal, roughness and metalness map alpha
channels (one for unavailable maps). Combine it with `dest.opacity`, which already includes the
base map and alpha mask. No CPU pixel reads are needed. This provides a fallback for damage textures without
an explicit opacity mask.

[Destruction](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/destruction.html) uses matching normal, roughness, AO, and opacity maps from one selected
material. Its roughness multiplies the copied surface roughness, while the surface supplies color and metalness.
The opacity mask blends the resulting damage lighting over the original surface once, avoiding a second alpha
interpolation of individual channels. `material.normalScale.setScalar(2)` strengthens the impact normals.
[Doppler Bullet](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/dopplerBullet.html) uses the same coverage approach with albedo alpha and a bullet-hole
roughness map. Its damage albedo is tinted by the sampled surface color, and its roughness replaces the surface
roughness within the mark. Both preserve the surface's normal detail alongside the damage normals.

## Sample a Channel Again

```ts
materialComposite: (source, dest, context) => ({
  color: context.sampleSource('color', `(${context.sourceUV} + vec2(0.01, 0.0))`),
  normal: dest.normal,
}),
materialCompositeGPU: (source, dest, context) => ({
  color: context.sampleSource('color', context.sourceUV.add(vec2(0.01, 0))),
  normal: dest.normal,
}),
```

`sourceUV` is the selected source chart coordinate before map transforms and atlas placement.
Resampling preserves material selection, map transforms, wrapping and atlas aliases. Request any
supported channel repeatedly at different coordinates. Unused source nodes are omitted from the
TSL shader graph. All sampling happens on the GPU; there is no canvas pixel readback.

`sampleDest(channel, coordinates)` resamples destination inputs where supported. The GLSL path
supports built-in color/opacity maps and standard roughness/metalness maps; destination normal
resampling falls back to the current destination normal. TSL resampling uses the destination
node's UV context; nodes with explicit fixed UVs retain those UVs. `destUV` is the renderer's
original texture coordinate. Alpha testing, clipping and ordinary lighting continue through the
destination renderer's material stages.

See [Destruction](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/destruction.html) for collision UV patches, atlas constraints,
mesh variation and an example rendered with both backends.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/module-priority.md -->

# Module Priority and Execution Order

RZMPS sorts modules and generic spatial effects together by numeric priority. Smaller priorities run first within a phase. Input order is preserved for equal priorities. A module's `dependents` are flattened before sorting; each dependent's own priority still determines its phase.

| Priority | Phase | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less than 0 | Before movement | Changes become permanent simulation state |
| 0 up to, excluding, 1 | Before movement | Transient changes influence this frame's movement |
| 1 or greater | After movement | Transient changes affect this frame's rendered appearance |

Use `Module.Priority.Permanent` (`-1`) for acceleration or accumulated changes. Multiply acceleration by `deltaTime` so the change is expressed per second. Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` (`0.5`) for a temporary velocity adjustment that should influence integration without accumulating into next frame's base velocity. Use `Module.Priority.Transient` (`1`) for a size or tint multiplier derived from normalized particle age.

At the beginning of the next update, cached values are restored. A render-time velocity change therefore does not move the particle in the current frame, and it does not automatically become next frame's velocity. This is why changing the priority can change the meaning of an otherwise identical callback.

Prefer a built-in lifetime module before writing an equivalent callback: those modules already select phases appropriate to their behavior. When combining modifiers that write the same property, inspect both their priorities and whether each callback assigns or multiplies that property. A later assignment can replace an earlier result.

`prepare(context)` runs before the per-particle phase. Use it for shared calculations or spatial collection, and reuse
scratch objects in the particle callback. Population LOD removes simulated particles before module work; surviving
particles run every step.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/particle-octree.md -->

# Particle Spatial Acceleration

RZMPS provides complementary structures for particle-to-particle work:

| Operation | `ParticleOctree` (CPU) | `ParticleSpatialGrid` (GPU) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bounds | `setBounds`, `bounds` | `setBounds`, `bounds` |
| Resolution | `maxDepth`, `particlesPerLeaf` | `maxDepth`, brick/cell subdivisions |
| Update | `rebuild(particles, tags?)` | `rebuild(renderer, buffers, token?)` |
| Position lookup | `locate(position)` returns a node | `locate(position)` returns a cell coordinate |
| Radius query | `particlesInRadius` array | `forEachParticleInRadius` TSL visitor |
| Quality | `timeQuality` | `timeQuality` |
| Cleanup | garbage-collected CPU data | `dispose(renderer?)` / `destroy(renderer?)` |

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU comparisons, neighborhood queries, and aggregate approximations. Use
`ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU comparisons and exact-radius shader queries. They share conceptual
configuration names where the meanings match, but their results are intentionally different:
octree queries return CPU particle arrays and expose aggregates, while grid queries emit shader work and never
materialize a JavaScript particle array.

## CPU: ParticleOctree

`ParticleOctree<TAggregate>` groups particle positions into cubic cells and computes an application-defined aggregate. It supports exact-radius queries as well as aggregate approximations. It is separate from mesh collision acceleration: its entries are particle indices, not triangle faces.

Supply a configuration and an aggregator with `new` and `combine` functions. `new` must handle an absent particle because the tree asks it for an empty node aggregate. `combine` merges aggregates; return independent state or carefully manage mutation so sibling nodes cannot corrupt one another.

```ts
import { ParticleOctree } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const tree = new ParticleOctree<number>({
  maxDepth: 6,
  particlesPerLeaf: 8,
  timeQuality: 1,
}, {
  new: (particle) => particle ? 1 : 0,
  combine: (a, b) => a + b,
});

tree.setBounds(system.boundingBox);
tree.rebuild(system.particles);
const node = tree.locate(system.particles[0].position);
const neighbors = tree.particlesInRadius(
  system.particles[0].position,
  2,
  { excludeIndex: 0 },
);
```

Guard the last line when the population is empty. `rebuild` accepts an optional tag selection. Only particles inside the resolved bounds and matching that selection contribute. Choose bounds in the same coordinate space as particle positions. Call `setBounds` when your population moves beyond the original volume; `locate` returns the root for a position outside the tree, which is not a nearest-neighbor result.

`maxDepth` defaults to 8 and `particlesPerLeaf` to 4. Deeper trees reduce cell size but increase node construction and neighbor bookkeeping. Increasing leaf capacity limits subdivision in dense populations. `timeQuality` defaults to 1; values below 1 skip some rebuilds after the first build. Check the boolean return from `rebuild` before assuming aggregates describe the current frame.

`particlesInRadius` prunes nodes using sphere-AABB intersection before exact distance tests in
leaf nodes. It is typically `O(log n + k)` for a balanced tree and `k` results, with an `O(n)`
worst case for broad queries or degenerate distributions. Options can exclude one particle index
and require matching tags. Queries use the population and node placement from the last successful
rebuild, so throttled trees may omit particles that have since crossed into the query volume.

`getNodes()` returns a new array of node references. Nodes expose bounds, neighbors, aggregate, and indices into the particle array passed to the last successful rebuild. Rebuilds replace node identities; do not retain nodes across rebuilds. Treat skipped rebuild data as stale if particles have been removed or reordered. `quantizeBounds` can stabilize moving bounds to reduce spatial churn, at the cost of looser bounds.

The [Boids example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/boids.html) demonstrates aggregation in a complete effect. Profile construction as well as query costs before increasing depth or rebuild frequency.

## GPU: ParticleSpatialGrid

Modules normally request a managed grid instead of constructing one. Set `useSpatialGrid: true`
for defaults or pass construction options through `spatialGridOptions`; the module's `modifyGPU` callback receives the
grid through `context.spatialGrid`. The equivalent CPU callback reads `context.octree` when
`useOctree` or `octreeOptions` is configured. Boids uses this managed lifecycle with its own
aggregate format and includes particle-affector source tags in the tree population;
its GPU grid uses the same managed acquisition and cleanup as other modules.

```ts
const neighbors = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, { system, octree }) => {
    const neighbors = octree.particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2);
    // Compare CPU neighbors; skip particle itself when needed.
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    useSpatialGrid: true,
    spatialGridOptions: { brickSubdivisions: 3, cellSubdivisions: 4 },
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, { spatialGrid: grid }) => {
      grid?.forEachParticleInRadius(
        particle.position,
        float(2),
        (neighbor, distanceSquared) => {
          // Build TSL operations using neighbor and distanceSquared.
        },
        { excludeIndex: particle.index },
      );
    },
  },
);
```

Custom infrastructure can instantiate `ParticleSpatialGrid` directly, call `rebuild` with a
WebGPU renderer and `GPUParticleBufferState`, then dispose it explicitly. A positive
`maxQuerySteps` truncates traversal; zero is unbounded. Automatic bounds expansion prevents lost
particles, but because the number of cells is fixed, expanding bounds increases cell size and
reduces spatial resolution. Keep bounds tight enough for the expected population and use
`readDiagnostics` only for validation or profiling because it performs asynchronous GPU readback.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/renderer-children-lod.md -->

# Renderer Children and Population LOD

Set `ParticleSystem.lod` to reduce simulated population with distance. The system calculates one `quality` value from zero through one and shares it with every emitter and renderer.

```ts
import { CompensationMode, Emitter, ParticleSystem, SpriteRenderer, LightRenderer } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const system = new ParticleSystem({
  lod: { distance: 20, quality: 0.5, maxLevel: 3, continuous: true },
  emitters: new Emitter({ rate: 200 }),
  renderers: new SpriteRenderer(undefined, {
    children: {
      count: 2,
      radius: 0.5,
      scale: [1, 0.6],
      alpha: [0.9, 0.5],
      randomizeScale: 0.2,
      randomizeAlpha: 0.15,
      radialFalloff: t => t * t,
    },
    compensation: CompensationMode.Children,
  }),
});
```

At quality 0.5, emission requests are halved before particles are allocated. Each birth receives a random priority below its birth quality, independent of its ID. When quality drops, particles at or above the new threshold are permanently removed before modules, movement, spatial queries, and collision. LOD removal does not dispatch normal death callbacks, death audio, or death subsystems. Surviving particles run every simulation step.

Increasing quality allows ordinary emission to restore density. Finite bursts may never recover their omitted particles. `simulationDistance` remains an independent hard cutoff, and `maxParticles` limits simulation capacity.

## Spatial grouping

`Renderer` can merge the eligible, tag-filtered simulation population into render-only
representatives. Sprites and meshes default to `count: -1` (unlimited), `ratio: 1`,
and `groupingRadius: -1` (unbounded). Lights default to `count: 50`.

The unlimited-count, ratio-one policy bypasses grouping entirely: no octree or
spatial grid is constructed, requested, rebuilt or queried for grouping. The GPU
helper is created lazily only when the configured target can reduce the input.
Empty populations also bypass it. A retained helper is unused while grouping is
disabled and is released on renderer reset. Independently enabled Children LOD
compensation can still request the system's spatial spacing data.

```ts
const lights = new LightRenderer({ count: 8, ratio: 0.1, groupingRadius: -1 });
```

For N eligible particles, the target is
`K = clamp(Math.round(Math.min(count < 0 ? Infinity : count, ratio * N)), 0, N)`.
Positive half-integers round up. A zero count or ratio produces no representatives;
negative count and positive Infinity are unlimited. K at least N preserves original
particles without CPU aggregation. This count is computed before artistic children.

The renderer builds a world-space snapshot of eligible particles in an aggregated
`ParticleOctree` on CPU or a multiresolution `ParticleSpatialGrid` on GPU. Its policy
distributes a K-anchor budget through occupied children in proportion to population,
stopping at regions assigned one anchor. This is adaptive population-weighted coverage,
not simply a ranking of the K most populated fixed cells. Cell summaries supply centroids.
CPU selection snaps to an actual source particle; GPU selection descends toward the
centroid and cooperatively snaps within a finest cell. Leaves receiving multiple
anchors choose distinct member slots, including coincident populations.
Every particle then contributes to its nearest anchor, exactly once. Anchors own
themselves to keep coincident groups nonempty. Identity breaks otherwise equal
spatial ties. Selection never consumes a dense region greedily.

A negative `groupingRadius` accepts every particle. A nonnegative radius limits
contributions to that distance from a selected anchor, measured in world units,
including the system transform for local simulation. Particles outside all
acceptance spheres remain unrepresented. K still requests nonempty representatives,
but finite radii cannot guarantee coverage of the population. Translating the effect
away from the origin does not change the radius.

Aggregates use weights `1 / (1 + distanceSquared / scaleSquared)`. The scale is the
positive finite radius when provided, otherwise the selected region's bounding-box
diagonal, with an epsilon floor. Position, color, alpha, scale, rotation, velocity,
and available age/render attributes are weighted averages; mass and visual
`Particle.contribution` are sums. Ordinary simulation particles have contribution
one. Lights retain their averaged brightness and alpha semantics: merging more
particles does not multiply a light's intensity by its membership count. A singleton retains its original values.
Simulation state, custom data and birth snapshots remain untouched.

All memberships and anchors are recomputed each update. Spatial regions and
weighted centroids improve coherence, but there is no stored group identity,
membership, temporal smoothing, or guarantee of continuous motion at split or
nearest-center boundaries. Renderers with identity-based histories can observe
anchor changes. Audio, trail and decal renderers retain their established `ratio`
selectors for sounds, trail histories and lifecycle projections; their shared
spatial grouping cap is `count` independently of those legacy selectors.
`DecalRenderer.count` continues to report live decals; its constructor's `count`
option supplies the preprocessing cap.

Grouping runs before artistic children, followed by LOD compensation. For example,
100 eligible particles grouped to four representatives with two artistic children
produce twelve visual instances, or twenty-four at quality 0.5 with Children
compensation. `renderedChildCount` counts only added children, never the population
removed by grouping. CPU compensation spacing still samples the original simulated
population; native GPU compensation resolves each aggregate's anchor slot in the
system-owned spatial spacing data.

CPU grouping uses source-octree aggregates for selection and a separate anchor octree
to prune nearest-center queries. It no longer performs grouping-specific Morton sorting
or range splitting. Identity ordering within selected regions makes CPU ties reproducible.
GPU grouping uses general sparse level directories and reductions, rather than a private
512-cell histogram or serial region heap. It maintains depths zero through four for its
source snapshot, then uses the existing coarse anchor hash for exact nearest-center queries.
The source and anchor indices are separate because they contain different populations.

GPU refinement processes independent regions in parallel at each maintained depth.
Generic aggregate construction and anchor snapping use cooperative workgroups.
Compact occupied-cell lists drive indirect scans and reductions; no construction readback
is required. The number of cached build passes depends on maintained levels and capacity,
not K iterations of a global priority queue. Final weighted memberships still use linked
lists and sequential per-group reduction, a remaining optimization opportunity.
Degenerate nearest queries can still inspect K anchors. Passes fit the portable
eight-storage-buffer limit. GPU grouping adds a compact world-space snapshot, optional
spatial directories/aggregates, and per-region selection scratch; ordinary single-resolution
grid users do not allocate these optional structures. CPU and GPU use the same
weighting formula but may choose different regions and anchors. GPU
scatter and linked reduction order can vary with scheduling, so float sums and
identity ties are not bit-for-bit identical between backends.

CPU scene lights read back only the compact GPU aggregates; grouping itself stays
on GPU. Lights are allocated predictively when the renderer is attached, using
`ceil(min(count, ratio * system.estimateParticleCount(tags)))`. Negative or infinite
count omits the cap; the existing default cap is 50. The estimate shares the particle
buffer allocator's `rate * lifetime + bursts` calculation, without its minimum
buffer size or power-of-two padding. Dynamic curves use the same conservative
sampling, cached per step. A manual population with no emission model falls back
to the finite count cap. Artistic children and LOD copies expand this predicted
reserve after the grouping cap, in the same order as rendering.

Reserved scene lights stay registered with `visible: true` and zero intensity
when unused. They are visually invisible, but activating an existing light does
not change the registered light count or trigger light-count shader variants.
If the actual output exceeds the prediction, the pool grows immediately. Rate,
lifetime, ratio or count changes refresh the prediction; unpredictable
movement-driven and subsystem emission can still require growth.

```ts
const lights = new LightRenderer({
  count: 18,
  ratio: 0.3,
  allocation: { shrinkThreshold: 0.75, shrinkDelay: 1 },
});
```

`allocation.shrinkThreshold` is the required-capacity/pool-capacity fraction below
which shrinking is considered (default 0.75). `allocation.shrinkDelay` is the
continuous time in seconds spent below that threshold (default 1). Recovery resets
the timer. The target is `max(predicted reserve, current render output)`, so idle
systems retain their anticipated warm capacity and surplus from temporary bursts
can eventually be released. The delay uses monotonic wall time and works with
asynchronous GPU readback; it does not count frames. Zero delay shrinks immediately;
`Infinity` delay or zero threshold disables shrinking. These properties are runtime
configurable and exposed in the demo's Light Allocation controls.

Grouping always precedes artistic children, which precede LOD compensation on CPU
and GPU. Optional level directories represent exact logical cells; hash buckets can
collide and must not be treated as spatial regions. The finest neighbor index remains
available. A system-wide live-slot list and selective occupied-bucket clearing are
separate potential optimizations, not prerequisites for these aggregate directories.

## Artistic children

The base `Renderer` expands its visual population before passing it to a renderer implementation. Each child inherits its immediate parent's attributes; only its position, scale, and alpha receive artistic modifiers. Children never enter `system.particles`, run modules, collide, or cause lifecycle events.

`renderer.renderedChildCount` reports additional artistic and LOD children. CPU counts update each frame. Reading this property during native GPU processing requests asynchronous diagnostics from the small counters buffer, at most four times per second; it does not read particle data back. The demo adds rendered and child totals to its particle counter only when children are present.

`count` is a timeless dynamic number: constants, ranges, and sets use deterministic per-parent selection. Counts are floored and clamped to nonnegative integers. They do not depend on age. A `[1, 3]` range normally produces one or two children. Zero is the default.

`radius` is the maximum spherical displacement, in particle simulation coordinates. Offsets remain fixed relative to the parent's position and do not rotate with its orientation. The default radius is zero.

`scale` and `alpha` are radial `ValueByParameter` multipliers. Numeric child multipliers are constants; ranges and callbacks vary with normalized radial distance. Both default to one. Each property's parameter is `clamp(distance / radius + randomize * (random - 0.5), 0, 1)`, followed by `radialFalloff`. Radius zero supplies distance zero. Randomization defaults to zero and easing defaults to linear. Scale and alpha use independent random streams, so changing alpha randomness does not move or resize a child.

Callbacks and easing use the existing GPU sampled-curve convention. TSL nodes are GPU-only and follow the existing dynamic-value compatibility rules.

## Compensation

`compensation` defaults to `CompensationMode.None`.

- `Size` multiplies visual scale by `1 / sqrt(quality)`, approximating constant billboard area. Simulated scale remains unchanged.
- `Children` adds approximately `1 / quality - 1` additional children to every original and artistic child. Fractional copies use deterministic selection. LOD copies inherit scale and opacity without further artistic modifiers.

There are exactly two generation stages. LOD children do not create further children. Quality zero generates no compensation copies. At quality 0.5, one simulated particle with two artistic children produces six visual instances.

The particle system owns compensation spacing. CPU views share a shallow `ParticleOctree` and cached per-root estimates; native GPU views share a `ParticleSpatialGrid` and a GPU spacing pass. The spatial structures inspect a bounded sample of local simulated neighbors. Estimates are retained for a root particle's lifetime to avoid offset jitter. Isolated particles fall back to their visual extent, so expanding system bounds cannot scatter compensation children. Spatial preparation runs only when compensation needs it, and CPU trees rebuild only when new roots need estimates.

## Identity and backend behavior

CPU particles expose `id`, `isChild`, `parent`, and `root`. Simulated particles have a null parent and are their own root. Child IDs derive from the immediate parent's identity and child ordinal. The base renderer uses `Particle.shallowClone(id, overrides)` for each visual child. Inherited vectors, colors, tags, custom data, and simulation snapshots are shared read-only. Each child owns its position; artistic scale modifiers and size compensation copy scale before modifying it. LOD children share their immediate parent’s scale and color. Child IDs use namespaced strings such as `root[0]`, `root[1]`, and `root[0][0]`. Artistic and LOD children share one ordinal sequence per parent; a root's LOD children follow its artistic children. Timeless seeded evaluation keeps counts and offsets stable across updates. Trails use the same stable child IDs to preserve independent histories.

Use `shallowClone` for a read-only view with selected replacements. Override vectors and colors are used directly, while unspecified references remain shared:

```ts
const view = particle.shallowClone('visual-copy', {
  position: particle.position.clone().add(offset),
  alpha: particle.alpha * 0.5,
});
```

`shallowClone` preserves the particle prototype and skips constructor work, ID generation, and new simulation snapshots. Renderers and custom consumers must avoid mutating shared attributes. Use `clone()` when independent mutable particle attributes are required.

GPU simulation contexts expose a computed slot/generation identity. Expanded render contexts resolve child identities and immediate/root views through one compact parent-index/ordinal mapping, with at most two hierarchy lookups. On GPU, guard dynamic parent access with `isChild`; original render slots resolve their parent view to themselves because shader-side null references do not exist. Simulation contexts have a null parent.

GPU-native sprites and meshes consume temporary packed visual buffers without reading child data back to the CPU. Artistic and LOD children occupy successive compact segments. Atomic allocation order may change packing, while identities remain independent of packing. Indirect draws use the GPU-produced visual range. Buffers are reused and grow in aggregate rather than reserving each parent's maximum possible count.

As with simulation storage, GPU visual storage has a practical capacity. The reusable arena reserves from the count distribution's mean, variance, and largest outlier and is bounded by `maxStorageBufferBindingSize`. Numeric TSL constants and uniforms use their current values; opaque GPU expressions reserve the full device-bounded arena because their counts cannot be bounded on CPU. Writes outside its capacity are discarded and counted internally. Very large or unbounded TSL count distributions should be avoided. CPU-input renderers expand children on CPU. With grouping enabled they read the compact GPU aggregates; otherwise their existing selective readback mechanism is used.

The generated compute and render shaders must fit the default eight-storage-buffer limit. `npm run preview -- --example lodStress --backend webgpu` records actual generated shader binding counts and active processing backend in its metadata.

Custom renderers implement `_update` for CPU input and `_updateGPU` for native GPU input. The public `update` and `updateGPU` methods perform base-class preprocessing before calling these hooks.

## Migration

Remove the former update-rate LOD settings from systems, emitters, modules, and renderers. Put distance/falloff/quality settings in `ParticleSystem.lod`. Replace renderer size compensation with `compensation: CompensationMode.Size`, or choose `Children` for density approximation. Emitter and renderer count selection are now coordinated by the simulated population; modules always update survivors at their normal frequency.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/spatial-effects.md -->

# Spatial Effects and Module Collections

A generic `SpatialEffect` is an Object3D containing a volume or custom test and a modifier. Add it to the same Three.js scene as the particle system. The system discovers scene effects when `useSpatialEffects` is enabled, then combines them with its modules in priority order. The effect's transform places its volume in the scene; RZMPS converts particle positions for tests.

The `spatialEffects` constructor collection supplies explicit effects in addition to scene discovery. `spatialEffectFilter` narrows the generic effects that can modify a system. Avoid using a broad filter that accidentally excludes your intended field. Use `tags` and `condition` on an effect to select particles after the effect has been selected.

Modules can collect scene effects for their own algorithms. Set `requireSpatialEffects` to one or more SpatialEffect constructors; `prepare()` traverses the scene and fills the module's `spatialEffects` list with matching instances. This is how specialized modules such as Boids can consume affectors without the affectors also acting as generic modifiers.

For a module, explicitly supplying `spatialEffects: []` deliberately gives it an empty collection and suppresses discovery. Supplying a nonempty collection limits it to those objects. `spatialEffectFilter` and constructor requirements still filter that explicit list. Distinguish this module-level selection from the system's generic effects list.

Use [First Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-spatial-effect.html) to build a field. For expensive selection, cache work in `prepare()`
rather than traversing the scene inside every particle callback. If you override `prepare()`, call
`super.prepare(context)` when you rely on the base spatial collection behavior.

On GPU, built-in analytic effects can be parameterized, batched, and indexed together. A custom
effect must provide GPU callbacks to run there; an unsupported generic effect is skipped rather
than forcing the whole system to CPU. Geometry-backed custom effects can use a baked inclusion
field, and `updatePolicy` distinguishes static, transform-only, and deforming geometry updates.
Optional system bounds filtering applies only to effects whose built-in geometry test guarantees
that bounds overlap is meaningful. See [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for callback signatures
and update policies.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/subsystems.md -->

# Using Subsystems

Attach a secondary ParticleSystem with `parent.addSubSystem(child, options)`. The parent owns its simulation timing;
update only the root. The child is reused across emissions, with separate emission contexts for parent particles, rather
than creating a new system for every event.

Choose `emitOnSpawn`, `emitOnDeath`, or `emitOnCollision` for event bursts. Use `emitContinuous` for a stream following
live parent particles. A burst emitter with `rate: 0` and a time-zero burst is a good starting point for a short event
effect. A continuous smoke emitter needs a rate and a lifetime long enough to leave a visible wake.

Inheritance factors control scale, lifetime, color, alpha, mass, and velocity transferred from the triggering particle.
Set `inheritLifetime: 0` when a death burst should keep its own lifetime; inheriting a dying particle's lifetime would
defeat the separate timing. Set `inheritScale: 0` when the secondary effect should retain a fixed world size. `ratio`
samples which parent particles emit; lowering it reduces child population and renderer costs.

## A death-triggered burst

Set `impulseAffectsCount` to scale every emitter in a collision run by
`impulseMagnitude ** impulseAffectsCount`. The default `0` leaves emission unchanged; `1` is linear
and `0.5` uses a square root. This multiplier applies to burst counts, rate and rate over distance,
and combines with population LOD before integer counts are allocated. Fractional emission credit
is retained within the emission context. Spawn/death events and continuous parent-following emission
keep their configured counts. The multiplier uses the triggering impact for the whole emission run.
[Destruction](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/destruction.html) uses square-root scaling to shed fewer fragments on weak impacts.
Both CPU and native GPU processing support this without additional storage buffers.

[Fireworks](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireworks.html) combines continuous rocket smoke and a death burst. [Metal Balls](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/collisionSubEmitters.html) combines collision sparks and collision audio. Inspect their source-linked system regions as well as their emitter regions: the child's lifetime, gravity, and looping choices are independent of the parent.

This child emits once for each parent death. Only the root needs an update call:

```ts
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { Emitter, ParticleSystem, SpriteRenderer, Textures } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const sparks = new ParticleSystem({
  duration: 0.3,
  emitters: new Emitter({
    rate: 0,
    bursts: { time: 0, count: 12 },
    radialSpeed: 2,
    initialValues: { lifetime: 0.4, scale: 0.06 },
  }),
  renderers: new SpriteRenderer(Textures.Simple),
});

parent.addSubSystem(sparks, {
  emitOnDeath: true,
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  inheritScale: 0,
  inheritVelocity: 0.25,
});

// In the scene's animation loop:
parent.update();
```

Subsystem emitters subscribe to their immediate parent's events by default. Their own particles dying do not
restart the effect. Use an explicit `eventScope` when another origin is intended. Child particles receive their
emitter's own tags; they do not automatically inherit source tags.

Collision emission needs a Collision module and collidable scene geometry or a configured collision backend.
`impulseThreshold` rejects weak contacts; impulse factors can increase spark scale or speed, and
`impulseAffectsAlignment` points emission away from the contact. Test in a collision scene: an empty scene cannot
demonstrate a contact-triggered effect.

[Fireworks](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireworks.html) combines continuous rocket smoke and a death burst. [Metal
Balls](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/collisionSubEmitters.html) combines collision sparks and collision audio. Inspect their source-linked
system regions as well as their emitter regions: the child's lifetime, gravity, and looping choices are independent of
the parent.

Destroy the owning root to clean up the effect. Do not also update owned subsystems from a scene traversal, or attempt
to reuse one child under two parents. Explicit frame advancement follows the same parent-owned event processing as
normal updates.

GPU-active roots schedule subsystem systems parent-before-child and keep native spawn, death,
collision, and continuous runs in GPU buffers. CPU listeners and CPU-input renderers receive
asynchronous event/readback data and can observe a small delay. A function-valued `shouldEmit`
cannot be translated automatically to a GPU predicate; inspect `getGPUEmissionSupport()` when a
custom subsystem selector is involved.

Registered sources and named custom events also drive these same subsystem contexts. Use `tags`
to select eligible source tags and `onEvent` for CPU or native GPU context handlers. See
[Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) and
[Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html).

## Event callbacks and emission context

Use `onEvent: ['flash']` to emit with the prepared context, or supply a callback to customize it. Callbacks can live
on the child emitter or in `addSubSystem()` options. Attachment options override the emitter configuration for that
relationship; an attachment's `onEvent` replaces the emitter's subscription map.

A CPU callback receives `(data, source, context)`. `data` is application-defined and typed as `unknown`; narrow it
before reading it. `source` is the triggering particle or registered source. `context` already contains the resolved
source transform and configured inheritance, expressed in the child's simulation space.

```ts
const flashEmitter = new Emitter({
  rate: 0,
  bursts: { time: 0, count: 6 },
  radialSpeed: 0.2,
  initialValues: { lifetime: 0.5, scale: 0.12 },
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  onEvent: {
    flash: (data, _source, context) => {
      // This event uses a number as its payload; other payloads fall back to normal strength.
      const strength = typeof data === 'number' ? THREE.MathUtils.clamp(data, 0.1, 3) : 1;
      return {
        scale: strength,
        alpha: context.alpha * Math.min(strength, 1),
        velocity: context.velocity.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, strength, 0)),
        duration: 0.25,
      };
    },
  },
});
const flashes = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters: flashEmitter,
  renderers: new SpriteRenderer(Textures.Simple),
});
parent.addSubSystem(flashes);

// A live parent particle or a registered source can trigger the same callback.
particle.emitEvent('flash', 2);
source.emitEvent('flash', 0.5);
// With no source ID, emission uses the producing system's origin.
parent.emitEvent('flash', 1);
```

The callback runs once per accepted event, not once per emitted particle. Its returned values are captured for that
emission run, including delayed births. Returning a partial context replaces only those fields; returning nothing
keeps the prepared values and still emits.

Context `scale`, `color`, `alpha`, and `mass` multiply the child's initial values. `velocity` adds a velocity vector;
`velocityScale` multiplies its initial velocity contribution. Context `duration` controls the emission run, while
`initialValues.lifetime` controls how long each child particle lives. The example's `scale: 2` therefore doubles
its configured `0.12` particle size without changing that emitter for other events.

Clone vectors or colors when deriving overrides from the context. For example, a built-in death event can emit
slightly above its final origin:

```ts
parent.addSubSystem(sparks, {
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  inheritScale: 0,
  onEvent: {
    death: (_data, _source, context) => ({
      position: context.position.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0.5, 0)),
    }),
  },
});
```

This supplies a named callback for the first example's death event. Returning only `position` also updates the
emission transform's translation; returning only `transform` derives the position from that matrix. A custom
transform should also be authored in the child's simulation space.

### Native GPU callbacks

For native GPU event emission, provide the corresponding TSL handler under `onEvent.gpu`. Configure both callbacks
before starting the system when the effect should support CPU and GPU processing:

```ts
import { float, vec3, vec4 } from 'three/tsl';

flashEmitter.onEvent = {
  flash: (data, _source, context) => {
    const strength = typeof data === 'number' ? THREE.MathUtils.clamp(data, 0.1, 3) : 1;
    return {
      scale: strength,
      alpha: context.alpha * Math.min(strength, 1),
      velocity: context.velocity.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, strength, 0)),
      duration: 0.25,
    };
  },
  gpu: {
    flash: ([payload], _particle, context) => {
      const strength = payload.x.clamp(0.1, 3);
      return {
        scale: strength,
        alpha: context.alpha.mul(strength.min(1)),
        velocity: context.velocity.add(vec3(0, strength, 0)),
        duration: float(0.25),
      };
    },
  },
};

// Inside a GPU module's modifyGPU callback:
particle.emitEvent('flash', vec4(2, 0, 0, 0));
```

GPU handlers receive shader nodes and up to three `vec4` payload values. Build calculations with TSL operations;
ordinary JavaScript conditionals cannot branch on a shader value. Native handlers operate on GPU event storage
without CPU event readback. A CPU callback alone does not become GPU code automatically. See
[Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) for payload and subscription details.

## Simulation frames

`simulationSpace` selects the reference frame for particle motion:

| Mode | Frame |
| --- | --- |
| `'world'` | Identity world matrix. Existing particles stay behind when the system moves. |
| `'local'` | The particle system's world transform. |
| `'transform'` | `simulationSpaceTransform`, supplied as an Object3D or world Matrix4; omitted means identity. |
| `'source'` | Each particle's emitting source transform. On a root system, this behaves like Local. |

Transform mode keeps a live reference. Moving the supplied Object3D, including its ancestors, or editing the supplied
world Matrix4 moves existing particles with that frame. The emitter still belongs to the particle system: its world
pose is converted into the selected simulation frame at birth. A source is a per-particle version of this relationship,
so one shared subsystem can attach particles to many moving sources.

```js
const pulses = new ParticleSystem({
  simulationSpace: 'source',
  sourceLoss: 'kill',
  // emitters, modules, renderers...
});
fireflies.addSubSystem(pulses, {
  onEvent: ['flash'],
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  inheritScale: 0,
});
```

Source particles keep their sampled offsets and independent motion while following source translation, rotation, and
inherited scale. `inheritScale: 0` keeps the attachment frame's scale at one. This avoids a follow module, source maps,
or storing source identity in application-owned particle attributes. Both registered sources and simulated particles
work; native GPU sources use slot and generation handles without copying their transforms through the CPU.

`sourceLoss` defaults to `'detach'`: an existing particle stops following the lost source and continues from its last
resolved pose. Choose `'kill'` for effects that should disappear with their source, such as firefly pulses. Reusing a
GPU
slot never reattaches an old particle to its replacement. Delayed births from a lost source are canceled; a death event
instead emits from its final snapshot and creates unattached particles. Singular reference matrices retain the last
usable frame for existing attachments. Use nonzero scales for emission.

Source space permits motion relative to the source. To pin a particle to its sampled offset, set the emitter's
`radialSpeed: 0` and leave its initial velocity and inherited velocity at zero; movement modules can also move it away
from that offset. The emitter's default radial speed is 1, including in Source space.

An explicitly configured child space survives parenting and parent space changes. A child with no explicit space
inherits its parent's mode, including its Transform reference when no child reference is supplied. For example, a
World parent gives an unspecified child World space, while an explicitly configured Source child stays in Source space.
Assigning `child.simulationSpace` also makes that child's choice explicit. This replaces the previous forced matching
of parent and child modes; emission converts between their frames when they differ. Changing the mode
or replacing `simulationSpaceTransform` preserves the world pose of existing particles; moving the referenced transform
moves the effect. GPU conversion takes place at the next simulation step.

Modules, particle positions, spatial queries, collisions, renderer inputs, and readback use a shared resolved coordinate
space: World uses world coordinates, Transform uses the supplied frame, and Local/Source use the system's coordinates.
Source offsets and motion are transformed into that common space before module updates. Consequently neighbor queries
can compare particles emitted by different sources, and scene forces act in the common frame. Use
`simulationToWorld`, `worldToSimulation`, and `getSimulationToWorldMatrix` for application conversions;
`resolveSimulationFrame(particle)` also includes a CPU particle's attachment frame. Three.js `localToWorld` and
`worldToLocal` continue to describe the Object3D itself. Particle orientation and scale use TRS decomposition;
compositions that introduce shear have the same approximation as Three.js Object3D transforms.

See [Fireflies](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireflies.html) for native Source attachments and
[Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) for registered origins and payload handlers.
